THE MEANING OF MEASUREMENT SCALES IN BUSINESS ANALYTICS
Labels and ranks
Nominal: unordered labels, such as order identifiers (IDs). Ordinal: ranked categories, such as OrderTier 1–3. Ranks do not imply equal gaps.
Differences and ratios
Interval: equal gaps, arbitrary zero (Celsius). Ratio: equal gaps, meaningful zero (elapsed minutes), so 20 minutes is twice 10.
Read the summary names
Mode: most frequent value. Interquartile range (IQR): middle-half width. Variance: spread using squared distances.
Percent change: change relative to the starting value. Choose a summary that fits the scale.

MATHEMATICAL ADMISSIBILITY BY MEASUREMENT SCALE
Mathematical admissibility means choosing calculations that have a useful meaning.

Nominal: unordered labels; count categories. Ordinal: ranked categories; compare order, but do not assume equal gaps.
Interval: equal differences, with an arbitrary zero, such as Celsius temperature. Ratio: equal differences and a meaningful zero, such as elapsed minutes; ratios are meaningful too.

The inclusion signs (⊂) indicate added mathematical properties. Numeric storage alone does not establish a scale.
Use the data dictionary, the guide to each field’s meaning, units and codes.

GC1015 | S03
Match meaning to calculation
WHAT CAN WE CALCULATE?
Match the calculation to the meaning of the variable
1
Check the scale
Mathematical admissibility means choosing a valid calculation: nominal allows counts; ordinal adds ranking and medians; interval adds means; ratio permits ratios.
2
Try two comparisons
Order tiers 1, 2 and 3 show rank, not equal service gaps. Tier 3 is not three times the service of Tier 1.
A 20-minute duration is twice a 10-minute duration. A 20°C temperature is not twice as hot as 10°C because Celsius has an arbitrary zero.
3
Use the meaning, not the format
Digits in a spreadsheet can label a category or measure a quantity. Read the field definition before selecting a summary.

SECTION 01 · DATA QUALITY
GC1015 | S03
One row, one stated observation
WHAT DOES ONE ROW REPRESENT?
Check the unit of observation before counting or averaging
1
Name the grain
Data screening checks grain, entry errors and missing values. Grain means what one row represents, such as one order or one item within an order.
2
See the counting problem
One order containing three items may occupy three rows. Counting rows would report three items, not three orders.
Conflating means mixing unlike units. Adding item rows and order rows can double-count activity and distort an average.
3
Check before calculating
Check the key (identifier expected to distinguish rows) for duplicates (repeated records). Then check each field. Missing age does not invalidate a separately recorded delivery duration.

=IF(ISBLANK(A2), "MISSING_NULL", IF(A2=-99, "SENTINEL_NULL", IF(A2=999, 
"SENTINEL_NULL", IF(ISNUMBER(A2), IF(AND(A2>=18, A2<=100), A2, "OUT_OF_BOUNDS"), 
"NON_NUMERIC_TEXT"))))
This separate age-screening example uses nested IF: one conditional test inside another. Read from the outside inward: blank, missing code, numeric value, then allowed range.
Null means missing. A matched test returns a label; a valid age passes through unchanged.
This example uses -99. LAB01 uses -1 for missing age and 999 for missing latency, the recorded delivery delay in minutes.
Keep valid latency even when age is missing. Use each variable’s own code rule.

SCREENING RECORDS AND UNDERSTANDING MISSINGNESS
Read the workflow and MCAR
Ingestion means importing records. An audit checks records; boundary screening checks allowed values. Null means missing, not zero.
MCAR (Missing Completely at Random): missingness is unrelated to observed or unobserved values.
MAR: Missing at Random
Missingness may depend on recorded information, but not on the missing value after accounting for that information.
MNAR: Missing Not at Random
Missingness still depends on unobserved information. The missing value itself may affect whether it is reported.
These are assumptions to investigate; a blank alone cannot identify its cause.

SECTION 02 · DESCRIBING
GC1015 | S03
Three ways to summarize center
WHAT MEASURES OF CENTER MEAN
Three summaries answer different questions
1
Mean: use every value
The mean is the sum divided by the valid count. For 10, 10 and 40 minutes: 60 ÷ 3 = 20 minutes.
2
Median and mode
The median is the middle ordered value: 10 minutes. The mode is the most frequent value: also 10. The 40-minute delay pulls the mean upward.
3
Read Metro’s evidence
Metro’s valid latencies have mean 28.4 minutes and median 22.0 minutes. The gap suggests upper-tail influence; it does not identify the cause.
Use the median to describe a typical order and the mean when every minute contributes to total workload.

MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY
Central tendency means the center or typical value. n is the observation count; xᵢ is one value; Σ means add the values. x-bar is the mean; x-tilde is the median. x₍ₖ₎ is the value at sorted position k.

Mean: add, then divide by n. Median: sort; find the middle, averaging two middle values when n is even.

For 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 minutes, both are 14. Replace 18 with 118: mean 34, median 14.
The mean uses every magnitude; the median depends on the middle positions.

HOW RESISTANCE AND BREAKDOWN POINTS OPERATE
Resistance: less pull from an extreme
One unusually large sale can pull the mean upward. The median, the middle value, usually moves much less.
Breakdown point: a stress test
This is the share of values that must be replaced to push an estimate without limit. One extreme replacement can break the mean; the median requires about half in large samples.
Keep the business question in view
Resistance is useful for typical experience. A genuine extreme may still matter for cost or risk; investigate it before excluding it.

SECTION 02 · DESCRIBING
GC1015 | S03
Read center, spread and shape
SPREAD AND DISTRIBUTION SHAPE
Center alone does not describe the customer experience
1
Dispersion: how much values vary
Dispersion describes how widely values are spread. Identical centers can hide different experiences: 20, 22, 24 and 2, 22, 42 both have mean and median 22.
2
Skewness: uneven sides
Skewness describes asymmetry, or unequal shape on the two sides. A right-skewed distribution has a longer upper tail, the region of unusually large values.
3
Kurtosis: the influence of extremes
Kurtosis summarizes tail heaviness: how strongly unusually distant values influence the distribution. Large values can signal more extreme observations. They do not identify an operational cause.
27
Concise Toolkit pp. 7-10

SAMPLE VARIANCE AND SAMPLE STANDARD DEVIATION FORMULA
A sample is a subset of the population, the full group of interest. Variance (s²) summarizes squared deviations from the mean. Standard deviation (SD, s) is its square root in original units.
A deviation is a value minus the mean. xᵢ is one value; x-bar is the mean; n is the count; Σ means add.
For 2, 4, 6 minutes: mean 4; squared deviations 4, 0, 4; variance 8 ÷ 2 = 4 square minutes; SD = 2 minutes.
The n − 1 divisor reflects degrees of freedom: after estimating the mean, only n − 1 deviations vary independently. Extremes strongly influence squared deviations.

SECTION 02 · DESCRIBING
GC1015 | S03
Keep units and valid counts visible
HOW SPREAD AND ASYMMETRY ARE CALCULATED
Use the same valid observations for every summary
1
Sample standard deviation
For Metro’s 9,958 valid latencies, sample SD is 13.5138 minutes. Subtract the mean, square each distance, sum, divide by n − 1, then take the square root.
2
Interquartile range
IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 31 − 19 = 12 minutes. It describes the width of the middle half, not the full range.
3
Skewness and the shape check
Cubed distances from the mean retain their signs. Positive skewness suggests a longer upper tail.
Near-zero skewness does not prove a normal, bell-shaped distribution. A histogram groups values into intervals to show their pattern.

INTERPRETING SPREAD AND SHAPE
Use the summary that fits the service question
1
Compare routine variation and extremes
Standard deviation uses all valid observations and responds strongly to extremes; IQR describes the middle half.
Metro’s SD is about 13.51 minutes and IQR is 12 minutes. These measure different features, so equality is not expected.
2
Choose a service limit with evidence
Setting a delivery-time limit requires more than center and spread. Inspect the observed tail and the service question before choosing a limit.

State the limit of the evidence
A 22-minute median does not promise delivery within 22 minutes. Examine the percentage exceeding a proposed limit and the cost of those delays.

SECTION
VISUAL EVIDENCE, HONEST DISPLAYS, AND DECLUTTERING
Compare bar charts, histograms and boxplots. A boxplot summarizes the middle half and flags unusual values. Remove decoration that makes evidence harder to read.
Chart Choice · Clear Labels · Visual Grouping

VISUAL CHOICE AND DISTRIBUTION GEOMETRY
Bar chart: compare groups
Use separate bars for categories such as hubs. A zero baseline means the value axis starts at zero, so bar lengths remain proportional.
Histogram: see the distribution
Group numeric values into intervals, called bins. Touching bars show how observations are spread across those intervals.
Boxplot: summarize and investigate
The box shows the middle half and its line marks the median. Whiskers are lines extending to observations within the calculated boundaries, called fences. Points beyond them are flags to investigate.
GC1015 · S03
38
Concise Toolkit pp. 11-14

TUKEY OUTLIER FENCE BOUNDARIES
Tukey fences are calculated boundaries for flagging outliers, values unusually far from the others.
IQR = Q3 − Q1. Lower fence = Q1 − 1.5 × IQR; upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.
Hub C: Q1 = 14, Q3 = 31, IQR = 17 minutes. Fences are −11.5 and 56.5 minutes. Zero is the physical duration bound, not the calculated lower fence.
Whiskers end at observed values within the fences. A flag starts an investigation; it is not proof of error.

SECTION 03 · VISUAL EVIDENCE
GC1015 | S03
Make comparisons easy to read
CHART GEOMETRY AND BASELINES
Make the picture support an honest comparison
1
Bar charts compare categories
Use categorical gaps between bars and start the value axis at zero when bar length represents amount. A shortened axis can exaggerate a small difference.
2
Histograms show a distribution
Group numerical observations into intervals, called bins. With equal-width bins, bar height shows count or proportion; touching bars indicate adjacent intervals.
Changing bin width changes the visible detail. State the units and inspect whether the main pattern persists.
3
Boxplots summarize and flag
Boxplots show a median and middle-half spread. Points beyond the calculated fences invite investigation. Software quartile conventions can differ; use the lab’s specified method.

SECTION 03 · VISUAL EVIDENCE
GC1015 | S03
Keep the evidence easy to find
COGNITIVE LOAD AND VISUAL CLUTTER
Help the reader find the evidence
1
What the reader has to do
Visual clutter competes for attention. Cognitive load is the mental effort needed to interpret the display, including finding labels, comparing values and remembering the question.
2
Simplify without losing meaning
Removing heavy borders, drop shadows and unnecessary gridlines can make a comparison easier. Keep useful labels, units, source information and meaningful reference lines.
3
Try a reading check
For a hub comparison, align the bars, use clear hub labels and reserve an accent for the relevant comparison.
Then ask: can a reader identify the measure, largest value and size of the difference without searching through a legend?

DATA-INK RATIO FORMULATION
Data-ink ratio compares marks carrying data with all marks in a graphic. The numerator (top of the fraction) is data ink; the denominator (bottom) is all ink.
Keep marks that help readers understand values. Remove decoration that competes with them.
Compare the original and simplified charts: can you find the labels, units and important difference more easily?
This is a design principle, not a score to maximize mechanically. Useful axes, context and accessibility may justify additional marks.

WHICH VISITS COUNT?
Worked teaching example: an OP-18b-style group
1
Define the group first
Illustrative records, not CMS results: five non-psychiatric visits discharged home lasted 145, 155, 165, 175 and 720 minutes. A transferred visit lasted 210 minutes.
Assume the five home discharges meet all other eligibility rules. This example excludes transfers; OP-18a would include them.
2
Calculate with the five eligible visits
Median = third ordered value = 165 minutes.
Mean = (145 + 155 + 165 + 175 + 720) ÷ 5 = 272 minutes. The long visit pulls the mean upward.
3
Explain the exclusion
Exclude 210 because of the chosen population rule. Retain 720 if valid: being unusually long does not make a record wrong.

REPORT THE RESULT RESPONSIBLY
Make the number understandable and comparable
1
Give the number a clear label
Report the median, minutes, eligible visit count, patient group and reporting period together. Name the OP-18 variant and the measurement rules used.
2
Show what the center misses
A lower median can coexist with very long visits. Examine upper percentiles and subgroup patterns; check missing timestamps before comparing hospitals or periods.
For our five-visit example: median 165 minutes, mean 272 minutes, range 145–720 minutes. Each summary answers a different question.
3
State what the result cannot prove
A shorter visit does not by itself prove better clinical care or explain why performance changed. Use additional evidence before making a causal claim.
